A remote build cache, and why the hard part is trust

The problem

Expand

CI rebuilds work it has already done. The cost is not the CPU, it is the fourteen minutes a reviewer waits.

Every pull request rebuilds the whole tree. Most of that output is byte-identical to a build that finished an hour ago on another machine.

CI spends most of its time rebuilding things that have not changed

A full build of the monorepo takes 14 minutes. A one-line change to a leaf package takes the same 14 minutes, because each CI runner starts from an empty working directory and no runner can see what any other runner has already produced.

Measured across one week of merges, 83% of compiled artifacts were byte-identical to an artifact produced by an earlier build. The work is not merely similar. It is the same bytes, computed again.

What it costs

Reviewer latency, not compute

Compute is cheap and getting cheaper. A reviewer who has context-switched away is expensive and does not come back for twenty minutes. The 14 minutes is the real number.

Why it persists

Local caches work, and do not travel

Every build tool already caches locally. That is why the problem is invisible to the person who introduced it: on their machine the second build takes nine seconds.

This is a worked example. The subject is invented. It exists so that the template has one document showing every component in a real argument rather than in a swatch, and so an agent asked to write a document has something honest to imitate.

The solution

Expand

One content-addressed store, written by CI and read by everyone. The cache key is the whole design.

Buildany runner, any laptop
→key = hash(inputs)
Cacheread, then write on miss
→immutable
Object storecontent addressed
trusted path writes need proof A hit is only safe if the key covers every input.

The cache is easy. Deciding what a cache key covers is the whole problem.

A remote cache is a hash map in front of an object store, and that part is a week of work. The question that decides whether it can be trusted is narrower and harder: what counts as an input? Miss one, and the cache returns a stale artifact that compiles, passes, and is wrong.

Sound

Declared inputs

Source files, the toolchain version, the flags. Hashable and complete.

Partial

Ambient inputs

Environment variables and locale. Enumerable, but only if you look.

Unsound

Undeclared reads

A build that reads the clock or the network cannot be cached at all.

The key is a hash of everything the build is allowed to read

A cache entry is keyed by a digest over the ordered set of declared inputs: the content of every source file, the resolved toolchain version, the compiler flags, and the target platform. The key is not the command line. Two invocations that differ only in argument order must produce the same key, or the hit rate collapses without anybody noticing.

Entries are immutable. A second write to an existing key is compared and dropped, never overwritten — so a poisoned entry cannot replace a good one, and a mismatch is a loud signal that some input is not in the key.

Input classIn the keyCost to addConsequence of omitting it
Source contentYes0Cache would be useless
Toolchain versionYes0Artifacts from two compilers collide silently
Compiler flagsYes1A debug build serves a release request
Environment variablesAllow-listed3Hit rate drops to near zero if all are included
Wall-clock timeUnsupported—Such a build is not cacheable. Mark it, do not cache it

Including every environment variable is the mistake that looks safest. It is technically correct and makes the cache useless, because CI_JOB_ID changes on every run and so does the key. An allow-list is the only workable answer, and it must be reviewed rather than guessed.

Architecture

Expand

A read is unauthenticated and cheap. A write is authenticated and rare. That asymmetry is the design.

1
Build
asks for a key
GET /cas/{digest}
Cache
2
Cache
302 to a signed URL
expires in 60s
Build
3
Build
on miss, compiles and offers the result
POST /cas with an identity token
Cache

Reads are open, writes are proved

The two paths have almost nothing in common, and merging them is the design error to avoid. A read is the hot path: it happens thousands of times a build, it must be fast, and the worst case of serving it to the wrong person is disclosure of a build artifact. A write is rare, and the worst case is a poisoned entry that every future build trusts.

Read path

Redirect, never proxy

The service answers with a short-lived signed URL and gets out of the way. Bytes never traverse the application, so throughput is the object store's problem rather than ours.

Write path

Only from a verified builder

A write carries a workload identity token that names the repository and the commit. A developer laptop may read everything and write nothing.

Entries age out by value, not by date

A fixed time-to-live throws away the entries worth keeping. The base image layer that every build reads is old and hot; a branch build's output is new and will never be read again. Eviction is scored on last access, not on age.

< 7dKeepread at least twiceretain
7–30dKeep if read since uploadscore
> 30dEvictnever read after uploadevict

The middle band is the one that matters. An entry uploaded and never read is the signature of a key that is too specific — it means some volatile input crept into the digest. A rising count in that band is a bug report about the key function, not a capacity problem, and the dashboard should say so.

AWhy not just use the build tool's own remote cache?

Two reasons, and the first is not the interesting one. The build tools in use here disagree about key derivation, so a shared store behind them would hold two incompatible namespaces.

The real reason is that their write paths trust the client. Any developer who can read the cache can write to it, which is acceptable inside one team and not acceptable once CI trusts the result. The write-side identity check is the part we cannot delegate.

BWhat happens when the cache is down?

Builds get slower and nothing fails. The client treats every cache error — unreachable, slow, malformed — as a miss, and a miss is just a normal build.

This must be load-tested rather than assumed. The failure that actually happens is not an outage but a cache that answers in 30 seconds, and a client without a short timeout turns a degraded cache into a broken build.

Build order

Expand

Four phases. The key function lands first and alone, because everything else encodes assumptions about it.

Phase 11The key function. Everything waits on it
Phase 23Read path, store, client. No shared files
Phase 32Write path and identity
Phase 42Eviction and the key-quality dashboard

The key function is the keystone, so it ships by itself

Phase one is one task. Not because it is large, but because every later task hard-codes an assumption about what a key covers, and a key function written twice is the most expensive rework available here. It also has to be the piece with tests before anything depends on it.

TaskPhaseWorkDepends on
BC-11The digest: input classes, ordering, the environment allow-list, and a fixture proving two orderings agree—
BC-22GET /cas/{digest} and the signed-URL redirectBC-1
BC-32Object-store layout, immutability, and the compare-on-rewrite checkBC-1
BC-42Client: lookup, a hard timeout, and treat every error as a missBC-1
BC-53POST /cas, workload identity, and rejecting laptop writesBC-2, BC-3
BC-63Upload from CI on a miss, and the poisoned-entry alarmBC-5
BC-74Eviction scoring on last accessBC-3
BC-84The uploaded-never-read metric, surfaced as a key-quality signalBC-6, BC-7

Phase two is three tasks wide only because BC-1 defined the shape they all build against. Attempting the read path and the client in parallel before the key exists is how two components end up disagreeing about what they are keyed on.

What would make this a failure

Stated up front so the answer is not negotiated later. A hit rate below 40% on merge builds means the key function is wrong and the project has not delivered, even if every task is closed. A single verified poisoned entry is a stop-work condition, not a bug to triage.

Open questions

Expand

Four unresolved decisions, each with what changes depending on the answer. None of them blocks phase one.

Needs a decision

Who may write

CI only, or trusted developers too.

Needs a number

Retention budget

Eviction cannot be designed without a ceiling.

Unknown

Cross-platform keys

Whether one key can span architectures.

Open questions

These are decisions, not research gaps. Each one has a cost that is not the author's to accept, and each is written so that a reader can answer it without reading the rest of the document.

1

May a developer machine write to the cache?

Allowing it roughly doubles the hit rate on the first build after a branch switch, because developers compile things CI has not reached yet. It also means the trusted store accepts bytes from an environment nobody attests to. Assumed answer: CI only, because a poisoned entry is unrecoverable in a way a slow build is not. Reversing this is a one-line policy change; reversing a poisoning incident is not.

2

What is the storage budget?

Eviction scoring is meaningless without a ceiling. At the measured artifact size and merge rate, an unbounded store grows by roughly 40 GB a week. The band design in Architecture assumes a fixed budget with pressure-driven eviction; a policy of "keep everything for 90 days" is a different design and a larger one.

3

Can one key span platforms?

If the target platform is in the digest, an arm64 laptop never reuses an x86 CI artifact, and the developer-facing benefit largely disappears. If it is not in the digest, the cache will eventually serve the wrong binary. Unresolved. The safe reading is to include the platform and accept the lower hit rate, but this has not been measured against real builds and the measurement is cheap.

4

Is a cache miss observable enough to debug?

A miss and a hit are indistinguishable in the build log today, which means a key regression looks exactly like a slow week. Nothing in the plan surfaces why a key missed. This is not a blocker, but it is the first thing anybody will ask for once phase two is live.

What is deliberately not being built

  • Distributed execution. A cache and a scheduler are different products. Reusing outputs does not require moving the work.
  • Cache warming. Predicting the next build's inputs is a research problem for a saving that eviction scoring mostly already delivers.
  • A UI. The hit rate and the uploaded-never-read count belong on an existing dashboard. A new web application is not warranted by two metrics.

An open-questions section earns its place only if the questions are real. If everything in it has an obvious answer, delete the section rather than padding it — and if the document has no genuine unknowns, say that in one line instead.
